title: Teams That Conduct an Occasional Hot Wash Promote More Candor
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece describes a structured debrief technique, borrowed from military and emergency-response practice, for processing genuinely failed projects: the 'Hot Wash.' It lays out the format precisely — everyone agrees candor is warranted, no personal blame is allowed, each person gets a fixed window to speak, and the leader goes first to model self-focused accountability. The author is explicit that this tool is meant for rare, high-stakes failures rather than routine after-action reviews, and that its value comes from proving to the team that direct, unfiltered feedback can be handled constructively. The piece frames occasional practice with this level of candor as a way to raise the team's tolerance for honest conversation more broadly.
points: The essay provides an unusually specific procedural template (ground rules, time limits per speaker, leader speaks first) rather than a general exhortation toward more honesty.
It draws an explicit boundary condition: the Hot Wash is for rare, high-stakes failures, not a routine practice, which protects its impact from being diluted.
The rule that the leader must speak first and focus on their own actions models the vulnerability the whole exercise depends on.
It links a single structured exercise to a broader cultural payoff — occasional intense candor training the team to tolerate more everyday candor.
quotes: A Hot Wash is an After-Action Review with a special set of rules. If used infrequently and only when necessary, this process can get to the heart of the issues and promote more candor for other team matters in the future.
The team leader insists that there is to be no personal accusation or blame directed during the discussion and that the team is to separate people and actions in their criticisms.

One speaker at a time, everyone gets five minutes to succinctly state what happened, why it happened, and what they would do about it next time to correct it. The leader goes first to set the example.
The “Hot” in Hot Wash refers to the immediate and direct feedback that occurs in this debrief.
Teams that occasionally engage in a Hot Wash learn that unbridled criticism in small doses can elevate learning and doesn’t have to be threatening or unsavory.
